CHAPTER XXI. THE FUGITIVE MOTHER

As I hastened along, a cloud came over the moon, and from the gray dark
suddenly emerged a white figure, clasping a child to her bosom, and
stooping as she ran. She was on a line parallel with my own, but did not
perceive me as she hurried along, terror and anxiety in every movement
of her driven speed.

“She is chased!” I said to myself. “Some prowler of this terrible night
is after her!”

To follow would have added to her fright: I stepped into her track to
stop her pursuer.

As I stood for a moment looking after her through the dusk, behind me
came a swift, soft-footed rush, and ere I could turn, something sprang
over my head, struck me sharply on the forehead, and knocked me down.
I was up in an instant, but all I saw of my assailant was a vanishing
whiteness. I ran after the beast, with the blood trickling from my
forehead; but had run only a few steps, when a shriek of despair tore
the quivering night. I ran the faster, though I could not but fear it
must already be too late.

In a minute or two I spied a low white shape approaching me through the
vapour-dusted moonlight. It must be another beast, I thought at first,
for it came slowly, almost crawling, with strange, floundering leaps,
as of a creature in agony! I drew aside from its path, and waited. As it
neared me, I saw it was going on three legs, carrying its left fore-paw
high from the ground. It had many dark, oval spots on a shining white
skin, and was attended by a low rushing sound, as of water falling upon
grass. As it went by me, I saw something streaming from the lifted paw.

“It is blood!” I said to myself, “some readier champion than I has
wounded the beast!” But, strange to tell, such a pity seized me at sight
of the suffering creature, that, though an axe had been in my hand I
could not have struck at it. In a broken succession of hobbling leaps
it went out of sight, its blood, as it seemed, still issuing in a small
torrent, which kept flowing back softly through the grass beside me. “If
it go on bleeding like that,” I thought, “it will soon be hurtless!”

I went on, for I might yet be useful to the woman, and hoped also to see
her deliverer.

I descried her a little way off, seated on the grass, with her child in
her lap.

“Can I do anything for you?” I asked.

At the sound of my voice she started violently, and would have risen. I
threw myself on the ground.

“You need not be frightened,” I said. “I was following the beast when
happily you found a nearer protector! It passed me now with its foot
bleeding so much that by this time it must be all but dead!”

“There is little hope of that!” she answered, trembling. “Do you not
know whose beast she is?”

Now I had certain strange suspicions, but I answered that I knew nothing
of the brute, and asked what had become of her champion.

“What champion?” she rejoined. “I have seen no one.”

“Then how came the monster to grief?”

“I pounded her foot with a stone--as hard as I could strike. Did you not
hear her cry?”

“Well, you are a brave woman!” I answered. “I thought it was you gave
the cry!”

“It was the leopardess.”

“I never heard such a sound from the throat of an animal! it was like
the scream of a woman in torture!”

“My voice was gone; I could not have shrieked to save my baby! When I
saw the horrid mouth at my darling’s little white neck, I caught up a
stone and mashed her lame foot.”

“Tell me about the creature,” I said; “I am a stranger in these parts.”

“You will soon know about her if you are going to Bulika!” she answered.
“Now, I must never go back there!”

“Yes, I am going to Bulika,” I said, “--to see the princess.”

“Have a care; you had better not go!--But perhaps you are--! The
princess is a very good, kind woman!”

I heard a little movement. Clouds had by this time gathered so thick
over the moon that I could scarcely see my companion: I feared she was
rising to run from me.

“You are in no danger of any sort from me,” I said. “What oath would you
like me to take?”

“I know by your speech that you are not of the people of Bulika,” she
replied; “I will trust you!--I am not of them, either, else I should not
be able: they never trust any one--If only I could see you! But I like
your voice!--There, my darling is asleep! The foul beast has not hurt
her!--Yes: it was my baby she was after!” she went on, caressing the
child. “And then she would have torn her mother to pieces for carrying
her off!--Some say the princess has two white leopardesses,” she
continued: “I know only one--with spots. Everybody knows HER! If the
princess hear of a baby, she sends her immediately to suck its blood,
and then it either dies or grows up an idiot. I would have gone away
with my baby, but the princess was from home, and I thought I might wait
until I was a little stronger. But she must have taken the beast with
her, and been on her way home when I left, and come across my track. I
heard the SNIFF-SNUFF of the leopardess behind me, and ran;--oh, how I
ran!--But my darling will not die! There is no mark on her!”

“Where are you taking her?”

“Where no one ever tells!”

“Why is the princess so cruel?”

“There is an old prophecy that a child will be the death of her. That is
why she will listen to no offer of marriage, they say.”

“But what will become of her country if she kill all the babies?”

“She does not care about her country. She sends witches around to teach
the women spells that keep babies away, and give them horrible things
to eat. Some say she is in league with the Shadows to put an end to the
race. At night we hear the questing beast, and lie awake and shiver. She
can tell at once the house where a baby is coming, and lies down at the
door, watching to get in. There are words that have power to shoo her
away, only they do not always work--But here I sit talking, and the
beast may by this time have got home, and her mistress be sending the
other after us!”

As thus she ended, she rose in haste.

“I do not think she will ever get home.--Let me carry the baby for you!”
 I said, as I rose also.

She returned me no answer, and when I would have taken it, only clasped
it the closer.

“I cannot think,” I said, walking by her side, “how the brute could be
bleeding so much!”

“Take my advice, and don’t go near the palace,” she answered. “There are
sounds in it at night as if the dead were trying to shriek, but could
not open their mouths!”

She bade me an abrupt farewell. Plainly she did not want more of my
company; so I stood still, and heard her footsteps die away on the
grass.
generated_text:
The moon vanished beneath a heavy cloud, plunging the world into a sudden, gray twilight. From the gloom emerged a white figure, clutching a child tightly to her breast, moving with a frantic, stumbling gait. She ran parallel to my own path, utterly unaware of my presence, driven by a terror that twisted every muscle in her frame.

"She is being hunted!" I realized, the thought striking me with cold clarity. "A predator of this nightmare night stalks her!"

To follow her openly would only add to her panic. Instead, I stepped directly into her path, intending to intercept whatever shadow pursued her. For a heartbeat, I watched her flee into the dusk. Then, behind me, a soft, silent rush erupted. Before I could pivot, a blur of white leaped over my head, striking me squarely on the forehead. I fell hard.

I scrambled up instantly, but all I caught of my attacker was a streak of vanishing white. Ignoring the blood trickling down my face, I sprinted after the beast. Yet, within mere steps, a shriek of pure despair tore through the quivering air. My heart sank; it was likely too late.

Pushing forward, I spotted a low, white shape emerging from the mist-laced moonlight. Initially, I assumed it was another hunter, but it moved with agonizing slowness, making strange, floundering leaps. It hobbled on three legs, dragging its left forepaw high above the ground. Its skin was shining white, marred by dark, oval spots, accompanied by a low, rushing sound like water cascading over grass. As it passed, I saw a stream of red pouring from the raised limb.

"It's blood," I muttered. "Someone else has wounded this thing before I arrived."

Yet, a profound pity seized me at the sight of the suffering creature. Even if an axe had been in my hand, I could not bring myself to strike. With broken, hobbling leaps, it disappeared into the darkness, leaving a small torrent of blood to flow softly back through the grass beside me.

"If it bleeds like this," I thought grimly, "it will soon be harmless."

Driven by the hope that I might still aid the woman—or witness her savior—I pressed on. A short distance ahead, I found her sitting on the grass, the child cradled in her lap.

"Is there anything I can do?" I called out.

At my voice, she jumped violently, ready to rise. I threw myself onto the ground to appear less threatening.

"You need not fear," I said quickly. "I was chasing the beast just as you found a closer protector! It passed me moments ago, its leg bleeding so profusely that it must be dying."

"There is little hope of that," she whispered, trembling. "Do you not know whose beast this is?"

Suspicious thoughts flickered in my mind, but I feigned ignorance. "I know nothing of this brute. What happened to its champion?"

"What champion?" she replied, confused. "I saw no one."

"Then how did the monster suffer such injury?"

"I smashed its foot with a stone—hard as I could strike. Didn't you hear her cry?"

"Well, you are a brave woman!" I exclaimed. "I thought *you* were the one screaming!"

"It was the leopardess," she corrected.

"I've never heard such a sound from an animal! It sounded like a woman in torture!"

"My voice was gone. I couldn't have shrieked to save my baby! When I saw that horrid mouth at my darling's tiny white neck, I grabbed a stone and crushed its lame foot."

"Tell me about this creature," I urged. "I am a stranger here."

"You'll learn enough if you're heading to Bulika," she said. "But I must never return there!"

"Yes, I am going to Bulika—to see the Princess."

"Be careful! You'd better not go... unless perhaps you are? The Princess is a very good, kind woman!"

I noticed a slight shift in her posture. Thick clouds had gathered over the moon, obscuring our surroundings. I feared she was preparing to flee again.

"You are safe from me," I assured her. "What oath would you require?"

"I know by your speech that you are not of Bulika," she answered. "I trust you. Neither am I of them; otherwise, I wouldn't be here. They never trust anyone. I wish I could see your face, but I love your voice. There, my darling is asleep. The foul beast hasn't harmed her. Yes, it was my baby she sought! And then she would have torn her mother apart for carrying her off!"

"Some say the Princess keeps two white leopardesses," she continued, stroking the sleeping child. "I know only one—with spots. Everyone knows HER! If the Princess hears of a baby, she sends her immediately to drink its blood. Then the infant either dies or grows up an idiot. I tried to leave with my baby, but the Princess was away. I thought I could wait until I was stronger. But she must have brought the beast back while I rested, crossing my path. I heard the *sniff-snuff* of the leopardess behind me and ran—oh, how I ran! But my darling won't die. Look, there isn't even a mark on her!"

"Where are you taking her?"

"Somewhere no one will ever find."

"Why is the Princess so cruel?"

"An ancient prophecy states a child will be the death of her. That is why she refuses all marriage offers, they say."

"But what becomes of her country if she kills every newborn?"

"She cares not for her country. She dispatches witches to teach women spells that repel infants and force them to eat abhorrent things. Some whisper she is allied with the Shadows to extinguish the entire race. At night, we hear the hunting beast and lie awake, shivering. She can sense the birth of a child instantly, lying in wait at the door to enter. There are words powerful enough to drive her away, but they do not always work."

As she spoke, she began to rise hastily.

"I doubt she will ever make it home," I observed. "Let me carry the baby for you," I offered, standing up.

She gave no answer. When I reached for the child, she clutched it tighter against her chest.

"I cannot understand," I said, walking alongside her, "how that brute could be bleeding so heavily!"

"Take my advice and stay far from the palace," she warned. "There are sounds inside at night, as if the dead try to scream but cannot open their mouths!"

With an abrupt farewell, she turned away. Clearly, she desired no further companionship. I stood still, listening until her footsteps faded completely into the silence of the grass.
